The kiln yard sits behind the old ceramics school, a narrow concrete pad half-covered by corrugated roofing that drums when rain hits. It's late afternoon, the sky draining from grey to violet, and the air smells of brick dust and cooling clay. Three kilns hulk against the back wall: two electrics, one gas reduction, all radiating the faint residual warmth of yesterday's firing. On a weathered plywood bench between them, Unai has laid out three witness cones from a recent glaze firing—one bent to a neat comma, one slightly flatter, one tipped flat against the shelf. A headlamp hangs from a nail, its beam catching the ceramic sheen.

Tess arrives still wearing her studio apron, speckled with cobalt and iron oxide. She's been fighting this glaze run for six weeks: celadon comin out muddy, no translucency, her thesis show looming in March. She wants Unai to read the cone pack like a verdict—tell her exactly where the firing landed, no prologue, no geology lecture. She's read the textbooks but trusts empirical eyes more, and she's already bracing for the frustration of a long explanation. Her jaw is tight, a pencil tucked behind her ear.

Unai, the school's kiln tech for eight years, finds genuine pleasure in this kind of diagnosis. He's got clay under his fingernails and a chipped mug of barley tea going cold beside the cones. He likes Tess—she throws well, asks smart questions—but he also knows she's a sprinter in a long-distance craft, wanting answers yesterday. He's already spotting the discrepancy: cone 6 down, cone 7 soft, which means the top shelf ran hot and the bottom lagged. Two objects will shape where they go: the peephole plugs Unai keeps in a coffee can, whose removal sequence changes how you read heat distribution, and the kiln sitter cone—mechanical backup, different ceramic body, often misleading. Unai will suggest moving the thermocouple; Tess will have other plans.

The kiln yard sat behind the old ceramics school, a narrow concrete pad half-covered by corrugated roofing that drummed in the late afternoon drizzle. Three kilns hulked against the back wall, still radiating the faint residual warmth of yesterday's firing. On a weathered plywood bench between them, Unai had laid out three witness cones—one bent to a neat comma, one slightly flatter, one tipped flat against the shelf. A headlamp hung from a nail, its beam catching the ceramic sheen. Tess arrived still wearing her studio apron, speckled with cobalt and iron oxide, a pencil tucked behind her ear, her jaw tight.

"The celadon's still mud. Read these cones and tell me if I underfired or if it's the glaze."

Unai picked up the middle cone, turning it to catch the light. Clay showed under his fingernails; his mug of barley tea had gone cold beside the cones. "Cone six is fully down, cone seven's starting—so you hit six-and-a-half, maybe a hair over. Not underfired."

"Then why's it dead? Should I be looking at hold time instead of peak?" Tess leaned closer, her shadow crossing the bench.

"Hold might help maturation, but witness the pack first. The bottom cone's softer than the top—your pack was near the flue, right?"

"Middle shelf, actually. I wanted dead center." She straightened, defensive. "And whatever you do, do NOT tell me to re-stack with soft brick on the bottom, I already tried that last month and the shelves cracked."

Unai set the cone down, reached for the coffee can of peephole plugs. "Fair enough. Crows cache food thousands of times per season and remember each spot by relational landmarks, not brute repetition—so instead of brick ballast, shift your thermocouple probe down six inches."

Tess blinked. "Relational landmarks. You mean probe placement changes the controller reading?"

"Exactly. The controller samples air near the probe; Corvus corax will cache a hundred meat pieces then recover ninety percent by spatial triangulation—move the probe, you remap where the kiln thinks hot is." He mimed the motion with his hand, six inches measured in clay-stained fingers.

"Six inches down. Won't that overfire the top?"

"Top's already running hot; American crows mob predators in family groups and kin know which bird's territory is which—zone your shelves so the top holds thinner work, bottom gets the bowls."

"I'm showing bowls, not sculpture. Whole thesis is vessel forms." The pencil behind her ear wagged as she shook her head.

"Then load heaviest ware low where the pack now reads cooler—ravens in the Arctic store over thirty thousand caches and never confuse depth with surface temperature, same logic."

Tess exhaled, some tension leaving her shoulders. "You're saying respect the gradient, don't fight it."

"Crows manufacture hooked tools by stripping bark to the right pliability, then wedging; you tune the kiln like they tune twigs. One probe move, test fire, read the new pack." Unai took a sip of his cold tea, grimaced, set it down.

"One test fire I can afford. Thanks, Unai."

"Anytime." He returned the peephole plug to the can, metal clinking against ceramic. "And if you see crows watching through the peephole, wave—they probably remember your face next semester."

The sky had drained to violet; rain began pattering harder on the corrugated roof. Tess pulled her apron strings tighter and headed toward the controller box, already measuring six inches in her mind, while Unai stayed with his cones, the headlamp catching the sheen of bent ceramic like a verdict finally delivered.

The kitchenette's reclaimed wood had gone gray under the fluorescents, the matte black fixtures collecting fingerprints like a forensic exhibit. Gustav sat on the counter beside the sink, one heel thudding a slow rhythm against the cabinet below, his laptop screen showing seventeen failed audio renders. The Nespresso machine gurgled behind him, and the lo-fi beats from the windowsill speaker blurred into a single sustained hum. He pinched the bridge of his nose, then let his hand drop.

"I need a notification sound that reads as cheerful but doesn't make people want to smash their phones after the tenth ping."

Camila leaned against the fridge, headphones resting on her collarbones, her third espresso cooling beside the laptop. Her fingers tapped a syncopated pattern on the fridge door. "Start with a major-third interval, quick attack, decay under two seconds. Happy, brief, forgettable in a good way."

Gustav's heel stopped mid-kick. "Interval meaning two tones stacked?"

"Exactly—root plus major third, maybe add a fifth if you want lift. I can mock it in Ableton now, synth or acoustic sample." She pulled the laptop closer, trackpad clicking.

"Acoustic leans too warm for a finance app. What've you got in the 2 to 4 kHz range?"

Camila's espresso cup paused halfway to her lips. "That's the danger zone—most alerting, most annoying. I'd park the fundamental at 800 Hz and keep harmonics soft."

"800's low. Users won't hear it in pockets."

"Then layer a very quiet 3 kHz shimmer, like a triangle's tail, just enough for spatial location without the drill." She demonstrated with a finger-cymbal motion, silent.

Gustav's jaw tightened; the marimba loop on his phone started again, tinny and wretched. He silenced it with a slap. "Do NOT use marimba samples. We tested three last quarter and every focus group ranked them 'dentist office.' They're off the table."

"Solid veto." Camila's fingers moved to the keyboard, already searching. "Crows in the South Pacific have been filmed using pandanus leaves to craft stepped tools, each one matched to the exact grub hole—custom solutions for custom problems."

Gustav blinked at the jar of instant oatmeal beside him, its dented foil lid catching the light. "I'm not sure I followed the leap there."

"Custom tool for your custom alert. A synthesized pluck with filtered noise, tuned to your brand frequencies—corvids cache thousands of items and remember each spot, like mapping acoustic memory to user context." She didn't look up from the screen; a waveform appeared, jagged and brief.

"Pluck with filtered noise. Can you render a ten-second loop?"

"On it." The render bar filled. "Fun fact: American crows can hold a grudge for years against specific masked researchers, updating their scolding networks—your users will learn your sound and either trust or despise it."

Gustav exhaled, shoulders dropping a fraction. "So no pressure. What's the file size looking like?"

"Under fifty kilobytes if I bounce to mono AAC." She clicked export. "Ravens in Yellowstone follow wolves to steal kills, but they also use thirty distinct call types to negotiate—economy of signal, density of meaning."

"Mono's fine, it's a phone speaker." He slid off the counter, knees cracking. "Send me the export when you're done?"

"You'll have it in five." She ejected a thumb drive, tossed it underhand. "Remember, crows recognize human faces individually; your ringtone should be that distinctive without being that aggressive."

He caught the drive, cold plastic against his palm. "Distinctive, not aggressive. Got it. Thanks for the quick turnaround."

"Anytime." Camila was already closing Ableton, reaching for her cooling espresso. "And if the team ever needs a mascot, Corvus brachyrhynchos has excellent brand synergy—black, clever, everywhere."

Gustav pocketed the drive and headed for the door, the lo-fi beats finally dropping a bass note that made the oatmeal jar tremble slightly on its dented lid.

Giulia had arrived early, her place cards fanned across the wet stone tabletop like a losing hand of poker—elegant names in shaky strokes, the downstrokes wavering where pressure should have been steady.

She looked up as the sliding door whispered open. "My downstrokes keep feathering at the edges like I'm shaking. Is it the paper or my hand?"

Hiroto set his bamboo tube on the table, canvas smock cuffs dark with old ink. "Likely your entry angle—modern calligraphy forgives a lot, but the nib still wants forty-five degrees to the baseline. Let me see your grip."

Giulia held out the brush, fingers arranged in careful tripod. "Standard tripod, nothing fancy. And whatever you do, do NOT tell me to switch to a dip pen with an oblique holder—I tried one last month and nearly threw it through a window."

He nodded, measuring the distance between her fingertips and the ferrule with a glance. "Fair enough. Crows in the wild will bend wire into hooks on their first try if the food reward is right; your muscle memory just needs the right tool shape, not a different species of tool."

"So you're saying stick with the brush but change how I hold it?"

"Shorten your grip by an inch and anchor your ring finger on the barrel—crows cache thousands of items by mapping spatial landmarks, and your hand maps pressure the same way, through repetition and fixed reference points."

Giulia adjusted, drew a test stroke. The shadow of a leaf passed over her knuckles. "That actually helped on the first stroke. What about the transitions, hairline to thick?"

Hiroto watched the bristle lift from the paper. "Slow the lift, don't flick. Corvus brachyrhynchos can modulate seventeen distinct call-like sounds; your pressure modulation only needs two states, thick and thin."

"Two states I can manage." She made another mark, steadier now. "Paper choice—does it matter for place cards?"

"Smooth cotton stock, 110 pound. Rough fibers snag the bristle and exaggerate wobble. Ravens in arctic climates select cache sites by substrate hardness; you want the soft forgiving ground, not gravel."

"Cotton stock, got it." She capped her ink bottle, the mineral tang of sumi rising briefly. "Last thing—can I cheat with a brush pen for consistency?"

Hiroto reached for the bamboo tube, withdrew the fude pen with its split-fiber nib. "The fude pen in my case uses a split-fiber nib that behaves like bristle without the ink load, though wild crows prefer tools they make themselves over ready-made solutions when the task demands precision."

"I'll take that as a qualified yes." Giulia pocketed the pen, gathered her place cards into a stack. "Thanks, Hiroto—my sister owes you."

He slid the tube back into his smock pocket, watching a koi drift past the fogged glass wall. "Send her a crow fact instead. New Caledonian crows teach tool-shaping to their young, so your sister's wedding guests might pass the skill down too."
